source_text: Praestantissime Tatiane, ut cum efficacibus argumentis sive demonstrationibus sermonem atque disputationem de Anima tibi conscriptam mitterem; eaque in re nullis Scripturarum uteret testimoniis. Quae quidem docendi ratio etsi vera sit, et illis qui pie sentire velint, quavis humana ratiocinatione certior et ad probandum aptior; quia tamen id a me sic fieri cupis, non ut tibi ipse satisfacias, quippe qui iam ita sis instructus, ut Divinis et Scripturis, et traditionibus atque constitutionibus adhaereas, neque ullis humanis rationibus de sententia dimoveri te sinas; sed ad eos convincendos qui aliter sentiunt, et Scripturis divinis fidem habere nolunt; quadam autem differendi facultate homines disputationi eiusmodi haud assuetos circumvenire ac fallere nituntur. Quibus adductus sum rationibus, ut non, velut aliqua deterritus imperitia, hanc tractationem subterfugerim; sed tua in me confisus benevolentia, tuae promptius morem gesserim iussioni ac voluntati. Nosti enim pro tua in me benignitate atque amicitia, quae praeclara effecta sunt, ea in hominum lucemque proferre; quae autem minus recte dicta esse videantur, ea dissimulare atque contegere. Haec sciens, audacter me ad scribendum contuli. Ea vero differendi ratione et ordine utar, qua et illi, qui res huiusmodi profitentur, scienter ac perite inquirere solent. Primum igitur proponam, quo criterio anima secundum naturam apprehendi queat. Deinde, quibus rationibus esse ostendatur. Tum deinceps, substantia ne sit, an accidens. Deinde consequenter, corpus ne sit, an incorporea. Praeterea, simplex ne, an composita. Tum rursus, mortalis ne, an immortalis. Postremo autem, rationis particeps ne sit, an illius expers. Haec enim in Disputatione de Anima, ut maxime propria, et vim atque naturam eius melius exprimentia, inquiri solent. Ad ea porro, de quibus hic differendum erit, probanda ac confirmanda, pro demonstrationibus, notionibus illis utemur communibus, per quas rebus quae manibus tractantur, assensus comparari solet. Brevitatis vero utilitatisque causa, iis duntaxat nunc ratiocinationibus utemur, quae ad demonstranda illa, quorum fit investigatio, potissimum valent: ut manifestis perceptuque facilioribus earum notionibus atque probationibus instructi, promptiores occurramus repugnantibus. Hinc igitur sermonis nostri atque Disputationis ducatur principium.
thought_title: Opening address and plan of the treatise
orientation: Gregory opens the work by addressing Tatian, explaining why he agreed to write on the soul without scriptural testimonies and outlining the order of inquiry he will follow.
pass_a_gloss: Most excellent Tatian, that I might send to you a discourse and disputation on the Soul written out with effective arguments or proofs; and that in this matter I might use no testimonies of the Scriptures. This method of teaching, although it is true, and for those who wish to think piously, more certain than any human reasoning and more apt for proving; yet because you desire it to be done by me in this way, not that you yourself may be satisfied, since indeed you are already so instructed that you cling to the divine Scriptures and traditions and ordinances, and you do not allow yourself to be moved from your opinion by any human reasonings; but for convincing those who think otherwise and refuse to have faith in the divine Scriptures; and who by a certain skill in disputing strive to circumvent and deceive people not accustomed to disputation of this kind. By these reasons I was led, so that I did not, as if frightened off by some ignorance, avoid this treatise; but trusting in your goodwill toward me, I have more promptly complied with your command and will. For you know, by your kindness toward me and friendship, to bring into the light of men those things which have been done excellently; but to conceal and cover over those things which seem to have been said less correctly. Knowing this, I have boldly set myself to writing. I will use that method and order of disputing by which those who profess matters of this kind are accustomed to inquire knowingly and skillfully. First therefore I will propose by what criterion the soul can be grasped according to nature. Then, by what reasonings its existence is shown. Then next, whether it is substance or accident. Then consequently, whether it is body or incorporeal. Moreover, whether simple or composite. Then again, whether mortal or immortal. Finally, whether it is rational or lacking in reason. For these things are accustomed to be inquired into in a Disputation on the Soul, as most proper to it and better expressing its force and nature. Moreover, for proving and confirming those things about which there will be disputing here, in place of proofs, we will use those common notions through which assent is usually obtained for things which are self-evident. For the sake of brevity and usefulness, we will now use only those reasonings which are most effective for demonstrating those things whose investigation is being made: so that, instructed by their notions and proofs that are clear and easier to perceive, we may more promptly meet those who oppose. From here therefore let the beginning of our discourse and Disputation be drawn.

choices.why: The glossary fixes 'proofs' for demonstrationibus, and the context contrasts these with scriptural testimonies.
The glossary gives 'scriptural testimonies' for this phrase; rendering it as 'testimonies of the Scriptures' preserves the genitive structure and the contrast with proofs.
The glossary fixes 'common notions' for this term, which Gregory says he will use in place of proofs.
The glossary gives 'rational' for rationis particeps, and the contrast with 'lacking in reason' (illius expers) makes the sense clear.
The glossary fixes 'incorporeal' for this term, which is contrasted with 'body' (corpus).

pass_b_english: Most excellent Tatian, you asked me to send you a written discourse and disputation on the soul, using effective arguments or proofs, and in this matter to employ no scriptural testimonies. This method of teaching, though it is true and—for those who wish to think piously—more certain than any human reasoning and better suited to proving a point, is nevertheless what you want from me. You do not ask this to satisfy yourself, since you are already so instructed that you cling to the divine Scriptures, traditions, and ordinances, and you do not allow yourself to be moved from your conviction by any human arguments. Rather, you want it to convince those who think otherwise and refuse to believe the divine Scriptures, who use their skill in disputation to circumvent and deceive people unaccustomed to such debate.

I was persuaded by these reasons not to avoid this treatise as if frightened off by some ignorance. Instead, trusting in your goodwill toward me, I have promptly complied with your command and wish. For you know, in your kindness and friendship toward me, how to bring into the light of day the things that have turned out well, and how to overlook and conceal whatever seems to have been said less correctly. Knowing this, I have boldly set myself to writing.

I will use the same method and order of inquiry that those who profess such subjects are accustomed to follow with knowledge and skill. First, then, I will propose the criterion by which the soul can be grasped according to nature. Next, I will show by what arguments its existence is demonstrated. Then, in turn, whether it is a substance or an accident. After that, in order, whether it is a body or incorporeal. Further, whether it is simple or composite. Then again, whether it is mortal or immortal. Finally, whether it is rational or lacking in reason. For these are the questions that are usually investigated in a disputation on the soul, as being most proper to it and best expressing its power and nature.

For proving and confirming the points to be discussed here, I will use, in place of proofs, those common notions by which assent is usually obtained for things that are handled by the hands. For the sake of brevity and usefulness, I will now use only those reasonings that are most effective for demonstrating the things under investigation, so that, equipped with their clear and easily grasped notions and proofs, we may be more ready to meet those who oppose us. Let the beginning of our discourse and disputation, then, be drawn from here.

last_rejected.quote: as if frightened off by some ignorance
last_rejected.why: Latin says 'deterred by some ignorance,' not 'frightened off by'; 'deterritus' = deterred, not frightened.
last_rejected.fix: not to avoid this treatise as if deterred by some ignorance
last_rejected.ruling: 'deterritus' ranges from 'deterred' to 'frightened off'; 'frightened off by' is within normal meaning.

last_rejected.quote: This method of teaching, though it is true
last_rejected.source_quote: Quae quidem docendi ratio etsi vera sit
last_rejected.why: The concessive 'etsi... sit' (although it be) is flattened; the Latin presents a hypothetical concession, not a statement.
last_rejected.fix: This method of teaching, even if it be true
last_rejected.ruling: 'though it is true' adequately renders concessive 'etsi vera sit'; no meaning lost or changed.

problems.quote: those common notions by which assent is usually obtained for things that are handled by the hands
problems.why: 'Handled by the hands' is a literal gloss; the Greek likely means 'obvious/evident things,' not physical objects.
problems.fix: Replace with 'things that are self-evident' or 'matters within easy grasp.'
